title: A thousand years as a day (2 Peter 3:8–9)
hookLine: God is patient, not willing that any should perish

cards: In October you push tulip bulbs into cold dirt, cover them, and walk away. Then nothing. All winter the bed looks exactly like a patch of mud.
A neighbor walking by would swear nothing is happening there. Underneath, roots are going down in the dark, on a schedule no one can hurry.

By the time the second letter of Peter was written, Christians had been waiting a long time for Christ to come back in glory. The first generation was dying. And people were starting to look at the patch of mud and laugh.

teach.b: Peter quotes the mockers almost word for word. Where is this promised coming? Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything goes on just as it always has.
It's a reasonable complaint, and the letter takes it seriously, in two parts. First, time.

teach.h: A THOUSAND YEARS AS ONE DAY.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day."
Peter is borrowing from Psalm eighty-nine, ninety in most modern Bibles, which says a thousand years in God's sight are like yesterday, gone. God doesn't stand inside the clock the way people do.
What feels like forever from the mud is a single day from above.
Second, and this is the heart of it, the delay has a reason, and the reason is mercy. The Lord isn't slow about his promise, Peter says, as some think.
He is being patient with you, "not willing that any should perish, but that all should return to penance." Return to penance is the Douay-Rheims way of saying turn around, change your heart.
The Greek word for patient here is makrothymei, literally long-tempered. Everyone knows short-tempered: the flash, the snap. God, in this verse, is the opposite.
His fuse is a thousand years long. So the waiting isn't absence.

teach.h: NOT WILLING THAT ANY SHOULD PERISH.
teach.b: It's room: room for one more person to turn around, and maybe that person is the one doing the laughing. The Church still lives inside this waiting, and every Mass looks forward to his coming.
But Peter's letter turns the question around: the delay may be the kindest thing that's happening.

how: Catholics profess at every Mass that Christ will come again in glory, and Advent each year is a season of joyful waiting; the Church reads God's patience as time given for conversion.

o: he is distant, and does not notice
he is slow and late to keep his promises

games.q: God's long patience — tap the pairs.

s: Peter says Christ's coming is delayed because God forgot
he says God isn't slow about his promise; he's patient, not willing that any should perish.
the line about a thousand years echoes a psalm
Psalm 89 (90): a thousand years in God's sight are like yesterday.
the Greek word for patient here means long-tempered

games.q: people are laughing: where is this coming he promised? everything goes on as it always has. how does Peter answer?
o: God is patient, giving everyone time to turn around.
games.why: Peter says God's time isn't ours, and the delay is mercy: not willing that any should perish, but that all should return to penance.

practice: Bring to mind something changing too slowly for you, a habit in yourself, a person you love, a prayer that seems unanswered, and notice the impatience, the short fuse.

Now imagine stretching that fuse, a month, a year, ten, as if you knew the roots were going down in the dark. If you pray, ask for some of God's long temper; if not, just let the timeline grow longer.

wordCard.voice: Makrothymei, he is patient. Second Peter three: God's fuse is a thousand years long, and his delay is mercy, not slowness. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: he is patient (2 Peter 3:9), literally long-tempered: makros, long, and thymos, temper.

carryVoice: Your line: he is patient. The waiting is room, not absence. Day six hundred twelve, done.
